quests.sentenceWithBlank: Maya switched to a different tutor ____ her old one kept canceling lessons.
quests.completedSentence: Maya switched to a different tutor because her old one kept canceling lessons.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Because' introduces the reason for her decision - the canceled lessons explain why she switched. 'So' would reverse the logic, making the switch the cause instead of the effect.
quests.nativeTip: Ask yourself whether this clause explains WHY she switched, or what happened as a result of switching.
quests.example: Maya switched to a different tutor because her old one kept canceling lessons.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The delivery was delayed ____ a truck broke down on the highway.
quests.completedSentence: The delivery was delayed because a truck broke down on the highway.
quests.grammarRule: Reason vs Result - because, not so
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Because' shows that the breakdown is the reason for the delay. 'So' would wrongly reverse this, suggesting the delay caused the truck to break down.
quests.nativeTip: The truck breakdown is the cause here - think about which clause explains the reason, not the outcome.
quests.example: The delivery was delayed because a truck broke down on the highway.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Noah switched to running outdoors ____ he found the gym treadmill boring.
quests.completedSentence: Noah switched to running outdoors because he found the gym treadmill boring.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Because' introduces his reason for changing his routine. 'So' would incorrectly suggest that switching to running caused the treadmill to be boring.
quests.nativeTip: The boredom explains his motivation for switching, not a result of switching.
quests.example: Noah switched to running outdoors because he found the gym treadmill boring.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: ____ the client had already approved the initial design, the team moved directly to production.
quests.completedSentence: since the client had already approved the initial design, the team moved directly to production.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Since' introduces a reason treated as already known or given, common in formal writing like this. 'So' would reverse the logic, making production the cause rather than the result of approval.
quests.nativeTip: This clause states a known, already-established fact used as the basis for the next action - a common way this connector opens a sentence.
quests.example: since the client had already approved the initial design, the team moved directly to production.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: ____ attendance had dropped sharply this semester, the university introduced a new participation policy.
quests.completedSentence: since attendance had dropped sharply this semester, the university introduced a new participation policy.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Since' presents the drop in attendance as the established reason behind the new policy. 'So' would put the two clauses in the wrong order of cause and effect.
quests.nativeTip: The policy is a response built on an already-established fact - which clause is presenting that background fact?
quests.example: since attendance had dropped sharply this semester, the university introduced a new participation policy.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The app stopped receiving updates, ____ the developer had shut down the company.
quests.completedSentence: The app stopped receiving updates, since the developer had shut down the company.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Since' gives the reason the app stopped updating. 'And' would only add the fact about the shutdown without showing it as the cause.
quests.nativeTip: The shutdown explains why updates stopped - that's the reason, not a separate added fact.
quests.example: The app stopped receiving updates, since the developer had shut down the company.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: ____ he'd never used public transportation in the city before, David nearly missed his connecting bus.
quests.completedSentence: because he'd never used public transportation in the city before, David nearly missed his connecting bus.
quests.grammarRule: Reason - because (can begin a sentence, unlike so/and/but)
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Because' can introduce a reason clause at the start of a sentence, followed by the main clause. 'So,' 'and,' and 'but' link two complete clauses and can't be used to open a sentence this way.
quests.nativeTip: This clause gives a reason and opens the sentence - which connector can introduce a reason clause in that position?
quests.example: because he'd never used public transportation in the city before, David nearly missed his connecting bus.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: ____ the quarterly figures are not yet finalized, we will postpone tomorrow's meeting.
quests.completedSentence: since the quarterly figures are not yet finalized, we will postpone tomorrow's meeting.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Since' fits this formal, professional tone well, introducing the unfinished figures as the reason for postponing. 'So' would reverse the cause-and-effect relationship.
quests.nativeTip: This is a formal business message stating an established fact as the basis for the decision.
quests.example: since the quarterly figures are not yet finalized, we will postpone tomorrow's meeting.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: I canceled our coffee plans ____ something came up at the last minute.
quests.completedSentence: I canceled our coffee plans because something came up at the last minute.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Because' is the natural, everyday choice for explaining a reason in casual speech or texting. 'So' would reverse the logic, making the cancellation the cause instead of the effect.
quests.nativeTip: This casual message explains a reason directly - think about which everyday connector fits a quick, informal text.
quests.example: I canceled our coffee plans because something came up at the last minute.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The account was frozen ____ suspicious activity had been detected overnight.
quests.completedSentence: The account was frozen because suspicious activity had been detected overnight.
quests.grammarRule: Reason vs Result - because, not so
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Because' explains why the account was frozen. 'So' would incorrectly suggest the freeze caused the suspicious activity, reversing the real order of events.
quests.nativeTip: The suspicious activity is the reason for the freeze - the cause, not something that happened afterward.
quests.example: The account was frozen because suspicious activity had been detected overnight.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Elena pulled a muscle during her workout ____ she had to skip training for two weeks.
quests.completedSentence: Elena pulled a muscle during her workout so she had to skip training for two weeks.
quests.grammarRule: Result vs Reason - so, not because
quests.ruleExplanation: 'So' shows that the injury caused her to skip training. 'Because' would reverse this, wrongly suggesting the injury happened as a result of skipping training.
quests.nativeTip: Skipping training is what happened as a result of the injury, not the reason for it.
quests.example: Elena pulled a muscle during her workout so she had to skip training for two weeks.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: ____ the old bridge had become unsafe for heavy vehicles, the city closed it to truck traffic.
quests.completedSentence: since the old bridge had become unsafe for heavy vehicles, the city closed it to truck traffic.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Since' presents the bridge's unsafe condition as the reason behind the closure. 'So' would put cause and effect in the wrong order.
quests.nativeTip: The unsafe condition is the established reason for the closure, described before the main action.
quests.example: since the old bridge had become unsafe for heavy vehicles, the city closed it to truck traffic.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Grace didn't apply for the promotion ____ she doubted she had enough experience yet.
quests.completedSentence: Grace didn't apply for the promotion because she doubted she had enough experience yet.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Because' gives the reason behind her decision not to apply. 'But' would only work if the second clause contrasted with the first, which isn't the relationship here.
quests.nativeTip: This clause explains her reason for not applying, not a contrasting fact.
quests.example: Grace didn't apply for the promotion because she doubted she had enough experience yet.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: For the flooring, you could go with hardwood ____ choose something more budget-friendly like laminate.
quests.completedSentence: For the flooring, you could go with hardwood or choose something more budget-friendly like laminate.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Or' presents hardwood and laminate as alternatives to choose between. 'And' would mean installing both, which isn't the intended meaning.
quests.nativeTip: These are two flooring choices being weighed against each other, not combined.
quests.example: For the flooring, you could go with hardwood or choose something more budget-friendly like laminate.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The streaming service doesn't offer offline downloads, ____ does it support multiple simultaneous logins.
quests.completedSentence: The streaming service doesn't offer offline downloads, nor does it support multiple simultaneous logins.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Nor' adds a second negative fact using the required inversion - 'does it support.' 'Because' wouldn't fit since this isn't explaining a reason, it's adding another missing feature.
quests.nativeTip: Watch the inverted verb order after the blank - the same pattern you've seen with negative-addition sentences before.
quests.example: The streaming service doesn't offer offline downloads, nor does it support multiple simultaneous logins.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: She never spoke of her childhood, ____ those memories were too painful to revisit.
quests.completedSentence: She never spoke of her childhood, for those memories were too painful to revisit.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'For' is a formal, literary way to introduce a reason, always following a comma and never starting a sentence. 'Because' would also give a reason but reads more like everyday speech than reflective narration.
quests.nativeTip: This clause explains her reason in a formal, reflective style - notice the reason follows a comma rather than opening the sentence.
quests.example: She never spoke of her childhood, for those memories were too painful to revisit.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: ____ the negotiations had collapsed twice before, the diplomats were cautious about the new proposal.
quests.completedSentence: because the negotiations had collapsed twice before, the diplomats were cautious about the new proposal.
quests.grammarRule: Reason - because vs for (for cannot begin a sentence)
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Because' can begin a sentence with a reason clause. 'For' behaves like 'and' or 'so' - it must sit between two complete clauses and can never open a sentence, so it doesn't fit here.
quests.nativeTip: This reason clause opens the sentence - only a connector that can start a sentence like this will work.
quests.example: because the negotiations had collapsed twice before, the diplomats were cautious about the new proposal.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The judge dismissed the case, ____ the evidence presented was clearly insufficient.
quests.completedSentence: The judge dismissed the case, for the evidence presented was clearly insufficient.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'For' introduces the reason in this formal register. 'And' would only add the fact without explaining why the case was dismissed.
quests.nativeTip: The dismissal is being explained in a formal way, with the reason following a comma.
quests.example: The judge dismissed the case, for the evidence presented was clearly insufficient.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Can't make it tonight ____ my car broke down on the way home.
quests.completedSentence: Can't make it tonight because my car broke down on the way home.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Because' suits this casual, spoken-style message. 'For' would sound oddly formal and literary in a quick text like this.
quests.nativeTip: This is a quick, informal message - think about which reason connector fits everyday speech rather than formal writing.
quests.example: Can't make it tonight because my car broke down on the way home.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: He rarely returned to his hometown, ____ too many painful memories lived there.
quests.completedSentence: He rarely returned to his hometown, for too many painful memories lived there.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'For' introduces the reason in this reflective, formal style. 'So' would wrongly suggest his staying away caused the painful memories, reversing the real relationship.
quests.nativeTip: The second clause explains his reason for staying away, not a result of staying away.
quests.example: He rarely returned to his hometown, for too many painful memories lived there.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The factory closed its doors permanently in 1998, ____ the region's textile industry never recovered from foreign competition.
quests.completedSentence: The factory closed its doors permanently in 1998, for the region's textile industry never recovered from foreign competition.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'For' fits this formal, narrative register, introducing the reason behind the closure. 'Because' would also give a reason but sounds more conversational than this reflective, report-like tone.
quests.nativeTip: This reads like a formal historical account - the reason follows the comma in that literary style.
quests.example: The factory closed its doors permanently in 1998, for the region's textile industry never recovered from foreign competition.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The merger fell through at the last minute, ____ the two companies could never agree on valuation.
quests.completedSentence: The merger fell through at the last minute, for the two companies could never agree on valuation.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'For' introduces the reason for the merger's failure. 'So' would wrongly suggest the failed merger caused the valuation disagreement, reversing the real order.
quests.nativeTip: The disagreement over valuation explains why the merger fell through - that's the cause, not the result.
quests.example: The merger fell through at the last minute, for the two companies could never agree on valuation.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The two companies could never agree on valuation, ____ the merger ultimately fell through.
quests.completedSentence: The two companies could never agree on valuation, so the merger ultimately fell through.
quests.grammarRule: Result vs Reason - so, not for
quests.ruleExplanation: 'So' shows that the valuation disagreement led to the merger falling through. 'For' would only work if the reason came after the outcome, which isn't the order here.
quests.nativeTip: This time the cause comes first and the outcome follows - which connector introduces a result rather than a reason?
quests.example: The two companies could never agree on valuation, so the merger ultimately fell through.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The team hadn't trained together much before the tournament, ____ their coordination on the field was surprisingly strong.
quests.completedSentence: The team hadn't trained together much before the tournament, but their coordination on the field was surprisingly strong.
quests.grammarRule: Contrast vs Reason - but, not for/because
quests.ruleExplanation: 'But' captures the unexpected gap between limited training and strong performance. 'For' and 'because' would incorrectly frame the second clause as explaining a reason, which it doesn't.
quests.nativeTip: The strong coordination goes against what you'd expect from limited training - that's a contrast, not a reason or a result.
quests.example: The team hadn't trained together much before the tournament, but their coordination on the field was surprisingly strong.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: ____ several customers reported the same defect, the company issued a full recall.
quests.completedSentence: since several customers reported the same defect, the company issued a full recall.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Since' introduces the reason - repeated defect reports - behind the recall. 'So' would reverse the cause-and-effect order.
quests.nativeTip: The customer reports are the established reason behind the recall decision.
quests.example: since several customers reported the same defect, the company issued a full recall.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The itinerary looked exhausting on paper ____ every day of the trip felt perfectly paced.
quests.completedSentence: The itinerary looked exhausting on paper yet every day of the trip felt perfectly paced.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Yet' expresses this contrast between expectation and experience. 'Because' would wrongly frame the second clause as explaining why the itinerary looked exhausting.
quests.nativeTip: The trip's smooth pacing goes against how tiring the itinerary looked - that's a contrast, not a reason.
quests.example: The itinerary looked exhausting on paper yet every day of the trip felt perfectly paced.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Ben swapped butter for olive oil in the recipe ____ he was trying to cut down on saturated fat.
quests.completedSentence: Ben swapped butter for olive oil in the recipe because he was trying to cut down on saturated fat.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Because' gives the reason behind his ingredient swap. 'So' would incorrectly suggest the swap caused him to want less saturated fat, reversing the logic.
quests.nativeTip: This clause explains his motivation for the swap, not something that happened as a result of it.
quests.example: Ben swapped butter for olive oil in the recipe because he was trying to cut down on saturated fat.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The contract was voided immediately ____ one party had knowingly withheld critical financial information.
quests.completedSentence: The contract was voided immediately because one party had knowingly withheld critical financial information.
quests.grammarRule: Reason - because (no comma needed) vs for (comma required)
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Because' can join two clauses directly without a comma when the reason is essential to the sentence. 'For' is a coordinating conjunction that conventionally follows a comma, so it doesn't fit smoothly here without one.
quests.nativeTip: Notice there's no comma before the blank - which of these reason connectors needs a comma before it, and which doesn't?
quests.example: The contract was voided immediately because one party had knowingly withheld critical financial information.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: The twins refused to nap at the same time all week, ____ their mother rearranged the entire afternoon schedule around each one separately.
quests.completedSentence: The twins refused to nap at the same time all week, so their mother rearranged the entire afternoon schedule around each one separately.
quests.grammarRule: Result vs Reason - so, not because
quests.ruleExplanation: 'So' shows that the mismatched naps caused her to rearrange the schedule. 'Because' would reverse this, wrongly suggesting the rearranged schedule caused the twins to refuse to nap together.
quests.nativeTip: The schedule change is a direct response to the naptime problem, not the reason behind it.
quests.example: The twins refused to nap at the same time all week, so their mother rearranged the entire afternoon schedule around each one separately.

quests.sentenceWithBlank: Neighbors cleared the overgrown lot ____ planted a small community garden together the following spring.
quests.completedSentence: Neighbors cleared the overgrown lot and planted a small community garden together the following spring.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'And' links two related actions the neighbors completed as part of the same project. There's no contrast, reason, or result being expressed here, so the other connectors don't fit as naturally.
quests.nativeTip: Both actions are simply steps in the same larger project, without any surprise, choice, or explanation of why.
quests.example: Neighbors cleared the overgrown lot and planted a small community garden together the following spring.
